beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Boopesh M., and this video is about AI fraud detection, and one number that fools a lot of people: accuracy. Quick note: this is an AI voice reading my script. And every result you'll see comes from my own small experiment, on synthetic data.

beats.role_note: BLUF -- hesitant writer corrects the misconception
beats.narration_text: Here's the whole idea in one line. A high accuracy score sounds great. But when fraud is this rare, it tells you almost nothing.

beats.role_note: dot grid: 580 dots, 1 red; real dataset counts
beats.narration_text: How rare is fraud? In a widely used dataset of real card transactions, there are four hundred ninety-two frauds out of two hundred eighty-four thousand, eight hundred seven. About one in every five hundred eighty. Here are five hundred eighty dots. Just one is red.

Now meet the laziest fraud model possible. It says legit to every transaction. On synthetic data with the real fraud rate, its accuracy is ninety-nine point eight percent. Frauds caught: zero, out of a hundred forty-eight.

beats.role_note: confusion matrix as 4 boxes; recall and precision in plain words
beats.narration_text: So use a better scorecard. Sort every test case into four boxes: fraud caught, fraud missed, false alarm, and legit, correctly let through. Recall asks: of all the real frauds, how many did we catch? Precision asks: of all the alarms we raised, how many were really fraud? For the lazy model, recall is zero.

beats.role_note: lazy vs logistic vs boosted: same accuracy, different catch
beats.narration_text: Now two real models, trained on the same data. A logistic regression: ninety-nine point nine percent accurate, and it catches sixty-six of the hundred forty-eight frauds. A small gradient-boosted model: also ninety-nine point nine, but it catches a hundred twenty-seven. Nearly twice the fraud, and accuracy can't tell them apart. Recall can.

beats.role_note: precision-recall curve with a moving threshold; cost rule
beats.narration_text: Each model gives every transaction a fraud score, and you choose the cutoff. Lower it, and you catch more fraud, but raise more false alarms. At point nine, the boosted model catches a hundred twenty-six, with forty-nine false alarms. At point zero one, a hundred thirty-six, with a hundred eighty-nine. Which is right? Say a miss costs fifty times a false alarm. Then the cheapest cutoff is a low one.

The takeaway: when the thing you're hunting is rare, accuracy is the wrong score. Look at recall, precision, and the cost of each mistake. Now the honest limits. My data is synthetic, built to match the real fraud rate, not real transactions. Real fraud systems use far more signals, and fraudsters change their tricks over time.

Your turn. Paste this into Claude, with my script attached. Make a missed fraud cost only ten times a false alarm. Where does the best cutoff move, and how many frauds do you give up? A good answer shows the numbers, not just a story.
